Bought it in 1988, our first purchase on an office loan, cost Rs 3.5 L. We used it for 4 years when son and I stayed there for his very crucial 9th to 12th grade school education. After that only tenants stayed there. Our apartment wasn't taken care of by the numerous tenants. It looked pathetic with stained kitchen, washrooms and termites eating away wooden doors, leaking pipes. This is inspite of regular repairs and full professional cleaning, painting and acid washing of bathrooms whenever tenants changed. The last tenant was the worst of them all. Finally by 2018 we wanted to dispose it. By now it was 30 years old. There were many proposals to sell , demolish the full sixteen apartments and rebuild with each owner getting a new apartment and the builder getting a whole new floor added. But many owners refused to shift out fearing the usual delays in construction. Some were old and weak. My professor is an owner there. Meanwhile our flat fetched only a pathetic price of Rs 54 L maximum. We felt bad seeing our first purchase in such a dilapidated condition. It needed a complete rejuvenation. We owed our dear house this. So we changed the bath tiles, accessories, floor tiles, doors, all closets, got it painted . Now it looked brand new. Immediately we got a buyer for Rs 70 L. Luckily the construction quality of the pillars, columns of the 80s was good. People are still living there and will continue for another 15 years easily. 16.6.24

So, while a well-maintained apartment can serve you well for decades, be prepared for the realities of urban development and changing city landscapes. Ultimately, investing in a good property and maintaining it diligently can ensure that your apartment remains a safe and comfortable home for many years to come.

Question: What is your favorite subject in school? And what is your most disliked subject?
Old_Answer: How many of you will agree with this opinion of mine I do not know. I liked the subjects in school and college if the teachers /professors were good in teaching, encouraged us and were humorous . So liking a subject, scoring well in it, choosing a subject for higher studies are directly related to whether you liked the subject teachers especially in childhood and school years. So I changed my favourite subject each year depending on my teachers. Sometimes it was English, sometimes maths, sometimes geography, sometimes physics, chemistry and once even my 3rd language ! I usually hated History mainly because the history teachers, I had, made it so boring. Sometimes we had grumpy teachers too. We hated those subjects. But when I became a teacher myself, I taught the subjects with lots of energy and humour mixed in it . Thus my students felt light when learning even tough maths chapters. Hence my students liked all my subjects.. Maths, Science, GK and Art.. mainly because they liked me. It was a soul satisfying job for me. Question: My mother is old and can no longer live on her own. I want my mother to live with us, but my wife does not accept. What should I do?
Old_Answer: Does your wife love you? If she does she herself will give a good solution to this. Why doesn't she like your mother? Is your mother a sarcastic, dominating pest? If your wife doesn't like your mother at all and doesn't care for your feelings for your old, helpless mother.. Then accommodate your mother nearby your house or an apartment in your building or community. Arrange a full time cook cum maid. Visit her everyday. Give her company. She shouldn't be left lonely. Take your children too everyday. If you do not have enough money to arrange her accommodation, maid etc then please talk to her about your helplessness and admit her in any affordable OLD AGE Home. There are different ones based your economical level. Visit her often. Take books, fruits and snacks…whatever she likes. Loving couples accommodate, adjusting senior parents. Answer_with_writing_sample: This is a delicate situation that requires careful consideration of both your mother's needs and your wife's feelings. First, have an open and honest conversation with your wife about your mother's condition and the reasons you feel she should live with you. It's essential to express your concerns for your mother's well-being and the emotional weight of the decision. Listen to your wife's perspective as well; she may have valid reasons for her reluctance, such as concerns about space, lifestyle changes, or the dynamics of living together. Finding common ground is crucial. Perhaps you can explore alternatives, such as hiring a caregiver for your mother or considering assisted living facilities that provide the necessary support while allowing her some independence. If your wife is still opposed, it may be worth discussing a trial period where your mother stays with you for a short time to see how everyone adjusts. Ultimately, remember that both your mother and your wife deserve respect and understanding. Balancing these relationships is key; you may need to prioritize your wife's comfort while ensuring your mother's needs are met. It’s a challenging situation, but with empathy and communication, you can find a solution that honors both your mother and your marriage.
